title: Who owns this address?
instruction: Eight links that might come to you in a message. Tap the ones that DON’T belong to the service they pretend to be. Only the real owner of the domain decides, not how the address looks.

items.why: You read the domain from the right, up to the first slash: the end is overeni-uctu.top. Everything to the left of it was written by the owner of that domain themselves, even the word seznam.cz.
The end before the slash is seznam.cz. The word email on the left is just a subdomain that Seznam set up on its own domain. A real address.
The browser treats everything before the @ sign as a username, not as an address. You actually connect to prihlas-se.top.
Look closely: r and n next to each other look like m. A domain like this belongs to whoever bought it, and in small print on a phone you can hardly tell it apart.
The end before the slash is google.com; the word accounts is a Google subdomain. It looks technical, but it’s real.
The hyphen joins com and darky into one word. The domain is com-darky.top; Steam has nothing to do with it.
It looks suspiciously long, but microsoftonline.com is Microsoft’s real login domain. A strange look doesn’t prove a scam. The owner decides.
The domain is steamcommunity.com, and that’s Steam’s real community. The part after the slash (/id/ondra) only decides the page inside the website.

debrief: A rule that always works: find the first single slash after https://, throw away everything before the @ sign and read the last two parts from the right (for .cz, .com, .top). That’s the owner. The padlock (HTTPS) won’t save you: it only proves that the connection is encrypted with the owner of that domain. Even a scammer can get a certificate for free.
